newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries hover in London await US retail sales.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries hover in London await US retail sales.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were little changed in London on Tuesday, with few investors willing to enter the market at current levels, analyst said.
U.S. retail sales data due later in the session are expected to be relatively weak and any surprises there would provoke a strong market reaction, they said.

"We've had a quiet start to the day and prices are not straying too much from the close," said Charles Quigley, bond salesman at Chase in London. "We have seen better buyers, mostly of the derivatives persuasion but that has failed to move things significantly."
At 0957 GMT, the 30-year benchmark bond was at 96-24 to yield 6.88 percent, compared with 96-23 in Tokyo, 96-22 in New York.
Two-year T-notes were slightly higher at 100-10, versus 100-09 in Tokyo and New York, while the five-year benchmark bond was at 100-17, also up from 100-16 at the Tokyo and New York closes.

Analysts said the main focus for the market on Tuesday will be the April retail sales figures due at 1230 GMT. A Reuters survey of economists forecasts sees a fall of 0.3 percent compared with a 0.1 percent rise in March. Excluding cars, expectations are for a 0.1 percent rise, compared with a 0.5 percent rise previously.
Quigley said yields were now at levels which suggested credit markets were expecting bond friendly news.

"There is a fair amount of good news built into the yield curve with two-year notes having pushed to 6.25 percent or just below it, five-year notes resting around six-and-a-half and bonds at six-and-seven-eighths," he said.
To make a further thrust from here, to higher prices and lower yields, Quigley said the market would need to see not just bond friendly news but a really weak figure.

"We need either lower prices or some extraordinarily bullish news to bring in new buyers at these yield levels," he said. "Apart from derivative and swap house players, we have run out of new buyers here from fundamental players, and real investors seem to be content to sit where they are."
Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International in London, said the market was trading fairly optimistically at the moment in anticipation of relatively soft data.
"Anything which challenges that will come as an unpleasant surprise. The market is trading on the assumption that April is going to prove relatively soft because it is a tax paying month," he said.

Hannah added that investors would continue to watch the dollar's performance, and would also look at commodity prices which have become a more prominent focus after the recent rise in oil prices and the CRB index.
June T-bond futures were at 110-10 in automated trade, down 2/32 from Monday's Chicago settlement.
